prompts.research:
#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF)
Description: The Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF) is normally a triennial cross-sectional survey of U.S. families. The survey data include information on families’ balance sheets, pensions, income, and demographic characteristics. Information is also included from related surveys of pension providers and the earlier such surveys conducted by the Federal Reserve Board. No other study for the country collects comparable information. Data from the SCF are widely used, from analysis at the Federal Reserve and other branches of government to scholarly work at the major economic research centers.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

messages.content:
#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF)
Description: The Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF) is normally a triennial cross-sectional survey of U.S. families. The survey data include information on families’ balance sheets, pensions, income, and demographic characteristics. Information is also included from related surveys of pension providers and the earlier such surveys conducted by the Federal Reserve Board. No other study for the country collects comparable information. Data from the SCF are widely used, from analysis at the Federal Reserve and other branches of government to scholarly work at the major economic research centers.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

I'll research the Survey of Consumer Finances comprehensively, verifying details about its publisher, authority, history, and current status.Two more searches to round out data access details and the historical/archival dimension:# Research Report: Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF)

**Prepared for:** preservationists, data librarians, data scientists, and policy researchers
**Status of the description you provided:** Verified as essentially accurate, with one nuance (the "surveys of pension providers" component is historical — tied to the 1989 wave — not a continuing feature of the modern survey). Details below.

---

## 1. Dataset Overview

| Attribute | Value |
|---|---|
| **Title** | Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF) |
| **Publisher / Sponsor** | Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (Division of Research and Statistics, Microeconomic Surveys Section) |
| **Cooperating agency** | Statistics of Income Division (SOI), Internal Revenue Service / U.S. Department of the Treasury |
| **Data collector (since 1992)** | NORC at the University of Chicago (1983–1989 waves were collected by the Survey Research Center, University of Michigan) |
| **Frequency** | Triennial (every 3 years) since 1983; predecessor surveys ran 1946–1971 annually, plus 1977 |
| **Collection identifier** | FR 3059; OMB Control No. 7100-0287 (current approval expires **August 31, 2027**) |
| **Most recent public release** | **2022 SCF** (data released October 2023; ~4,600 families interviewed) |
| **Current activity** | **2025 SCF is in the field** (interviewing March–December 2025, extended into early 2026); summary results and microdata expected **late 2026** |
| **Access** | Free public-use microdata from the Federal Reserve website; restricted-use data via application (Standard Application Process); historical waves archived at ICPSR |
| **Unit of observation** | The U.S. "family" (primary economic unit); representative of ~131.3 million households (2022) |

The SCF is widely described by the Federal Reserve itself as **the only source of representative information on the full structure of U.S. families' finances** — balance sheets (assets and debts), income, pensions, use of financial services, work history, attitudes, and demographics.

---

## 2. Publisher and Institutional Context

- **Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System**, Washington, DC — the survey's sponsor, designer, analyst, and publisher. The work is housed in the **Microeconomic Surveys Section of the Division of Research and Statistics**, which the OMB designates as the relevant statistical unit for confidentiality purposes.
- **IRS Statistics of Income (SOI)** — a formal cooperating partner. SOI creates a specially edited file of individual income tax records (the *Individual Research Tax File*) used to build the survey's "list sample" frame of likely-wealthy households, under strict statutory confidentiality rules (Internal Revenue Code provisions on statistical use of tax data, 26 U.S.C. §6103). The IRS sees only a sampling frame; respondent identities are never shared.
- **NORC at the University of Chicago** — the field contractor since 1992. NORC recruits, interviews (in person, phone, or Zoom, ~100–110 minutes per interview, via computer-assisted personal interviewing on tablets), and is legally forbidden from giving names/addresses to the Federal Reserve or anyone else. Identifying information is destroyed at the close of each study.
- **Cost:** the current OMB clearance estimates **$7.6 million annual cost to the federal government**, with ~7,150 respondents and ~4,410 annual burden hours.

---

## 3. Legal Authority, Mandate, and Regulatory Framework

The SCF is **not mandated by a statute that names it**; it is conducted under the Federal Reserve's general statutory responsibilities. The Board's Legal Division and OMB filings cite:

- **Section 2A of the Federal Reserve Act (12 U.S.C. §225a)** — the "dual mandate" requiring the Board and FOMC to promote maximum employment, stable prices, and moderate long-term interest rates.
- **Section 12A of the Federal Reserve Act (12 U.S.C. §§263, 263(c))** — FOMC open-market operations conducted with regard to the general credit situation of the country. Household balance-sheet data directly inform monetary and financial-stability policy under these mandates.
- **Paperwork Reduction Act** — since June 15, 1984, OMB has delegated PRA clearance authority to the Board. The SCF is cleared as **FR 3059 / OMB 7100-0287**, renewed triennially via Federal Register notices (most recent final approval: 89 FR 61423, July 31, 2024).
- **CIPSEA (Confidential Information Protection and Statistical Efficiency Act)** — data are collected solely for statistical purposes under a pledge of confidentiality.
- **Privacy Act** — the ICR includes PII and requires a Privacy Act statement.

**Participation is strictly voluntary.** There is no penalty for refusal; interviewers may not substitute households, which makes each sampled case statistically precious (only ~6,000–7,000 families per wave).

---

## 4. History

### Predecessor era
- **1946–1971:** An annual *Survey of Consumer Finances* was conducted by the **Survey Research Center (SRC), University of Michigan**, for the Federal Reserve Board, focusing on consumer finances, saving, and credit. These are archived at ICPSR.
- **1977:** A one-off follow-up wave; also **1963** saw an earlier high-wealth survey (Survey of Financial Characteristics of Consumers) that informs the design lineage.

### Modern SCF
- **1983:** The modern SCF launches (3,824 households + supplemental high-income sample), jointly sponsored with HHS and other agencies; collected by SRC/Michigan with a paper questionnaire. This was the first U.S. survey since 1963 with a tax-file-based oversample of the wealthy.
- **1986:** Follow-up reinterview of 1983 respondents (the **1983–86 panel**).
- **1989:** Major redesign of questionnaire and sample design; methodology has been largely stable since. The 1989 wave included a **related survey of pension providers** (employers/plan administrators were contacted to verify pension details) — this is the component your description references; it has **not** been repeated in subsequent waves.
- **1992 onward:** NORC becomes the data collector; waves every three years: 1992, 1995, 1998, 2001, 2004, 2007, 2010, 2013, 2016, 2019, 2022.
- **2007–2009 panel:** 2007 respondents were reinterviewed in 2009 — a unique panel capturing household balance-sheet changes through the Great Recession.
- **2022 wave:** 4,602 interviews (3,298 area-probability + 1,304 list sample); 7 records deleted from the public file for disclosure avoidance (public file: 4,595 families × 5 implicates = 22,975 records). Sample design adjusted to improve coverage of Black, Hispanic/Latino, and Asian families.
- **2025 wave:** In the field March–December 2025; public release expected late 2026.

### Long-run harmonization
- The **SCF+** project (Kuhn, Schularick & Steins, *American Economic Review* 2020) harmonizes SCF waves back to 1949, enabling long-run wealth-distribution analysis. This is a third-party academic derivative, not a Fed product.

---

## 5. Methodology (what data scientists need to know)

**Dual-frame sample design** — the SCF's signature feature:
1. **Area-probability (AP) sample:** standard multistage geographic random sample (119 primary sampling areas); covers broadly held characteristics (homeownership, vehicles, credit cards).
2. **List sample:** drawn from SOI tax-derived records using a "wealth index" model stratified into seven strata, disproportionately selecting likely-wealthy families. This corrects for the concentration of assets (businesses, tax-exempt bonds) that a simple random sample would miss. ~98% of cases with net worth ≥$5M historically come from this frame. The **Forbes 400 are explicitly excluded** (their wealth would dominate estimates and threaten confidentiality) — a documented ~1.5–2.5% of household net worth is thereby omitted, which researchers sometimes add back from Forbes data.

**Key analytical structures:**
- **Multiple imputation:** missing data are imputed 5× → every family appears as 5 "implicates." The 2022 public file has 22,975 records for 4,595 families. *Failing to account for this inflates apparent sample size and understates standard errors.*
- **Replicate weights:** because the sample design details are confidential, variance estimation uses bootstrap replicate weights (file keyed to X42001). Correct inference requires combining imputation variance and replicate-weight sampling variance (Fed provides the SAS `MISECOMP`/`MEANIT` macros; Stata users use `micombine` / community `scfcombo`).
- **Analysis weight:** X42001 (scaled to population of families).
- **Response rates:** historically ~65–70% for the AP sample and ~30–35% for the list sample; the oversample structure also serves to correct differential nonresponse among the wealthy.
- **Disclosure avoidance:** geographic identifiers, detailed occupations, and identifying detail are suppressed/blurred in public files; a small number of records are deleted entirely. Restricted microdata are available only via application to the Fed.

---

## 6. Data Products, Formats, and Access

Hosted at **federalreserve.gov/econres/scfindex.htm** (waves 1989–2022, plus 1983 and the 2007–09 panel, with full codebooks):

| Product | Contents | Formats |
|---|---|---|
| **Full public microdata** | ~5,300 variables | SAS (CPORT & COPY/EXPORT), Stata, ASCII (with Excel/tab-delimited variable maps) |
| **Replicate weight files** | Bootstrap replicate weights | SAS, Stata |
| **Summary extract** | ~350 derived variables used in the Fed's Bulletin article; inflation-adjusted | SAS, Stata, **CSV** |
| **SDA online analysis tool** | Browser-based tabulation (Berkeley CSM) | Web |
| **Documentation** | Codebook (the questionnaire *is* CAPI code — a simulated text version of the MR Interview program is published), standard-error documentation, annual "changes" notes, flowcharts | TXT, PDF |

**Community/derivative ecosystem:**
- **ICPSR (University of Michigan)** archives the SCF series including 1946–1971 predecessors — important for preservation redundancy.
- **R package `scf`** (CRAN) automates download, implicate merging, and survey-weighted analysis; Anthony Damico's `lodown`/asdfree scripts have long served the same purpose.
- **Fed publications:** triennial *Federal Reserve Bulletin* article ("Changes in U.S. Family Finances…"), the SCF Chartbook, and FEDS working papers.
- **Integrated products:** the Fed's quarterly **Distributional Financial Accounts (DFA)** and the **Enhanced Financial Accounts** distribute the Financial Accounts' (Flow of Funds) aggregate wealth totals across demographic groups using the SCF as the distributional basis.
- **data.gov** catalog listing; CRS analyses for Congress (e.g., CRS IF12928 on the 2022 SCF).

---

## 7. Users and Uses

- **Federal Reserve / FOMC:** monetary policy transmission, financial-stability monitoring (household leverage, debt service), and the Board's triennial *Report on the Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households* complements it.
- **Other government:** Treasury's Office of Tax Analysis, IRS SOI, Joint Committee on Taxation, CBO, CFPB, and the Congressional Research Service use SCF data for tax-policy modeling (estate tax, retirement incentives), retirement-security analysis, and wealth-inequality briefings.
- **Academic research:** the canonical microdata for U.S. wealth-distribution scholarship — wealth concentration, racial wealth gaps, retirement preparedness, consumer credit, portfolio choice, entrepreneurship finance. Thousands of papers; foundational to the modern inequality literature (alongside tax-data work by Piketty–Saez–Zucman, whose top-share estimates are benchmarked against the SCF).
- **Journalism and advocacy:** SCF-based findings drive coverage of the racial wealth gap, student debt, retirement adequacy, and "K-shaped recovery" narratives.
- **Private sector:** financial-industry and consulting analysis of household balance sheets.

**Public benefits:** the only nationally representative measurement of *who holds what* — enabling evidence on inequality, household financial fragility, pension coverage, and credit access that administrative data alone cannot provide (tax data lack balance sheets; credit bureau data lack assets). Its findings have informed debates over Social Security, tax-preferred retirement accounts, student lending, and post-2008 and post-COVID household recovery.

---

## 8. Preservation & Data-Librarianship Notes

- **Format risk:** primary distribution in SAS transport and Stata formats; ASCII + codebook is the most durable archival form. The CAPI "questionnaire" exists only as program code (SPSS MR Interview) — for 2022 only a *simulated text rendering* is published, so instrument preservation is inherently partial.
- **Redundancy:** Fed website (primary), ICPSR (preservation-grade archive), and academic derivatives (SCF+) provide layered preservation.
- **Versioning:** files are occasionally revised post-release (the "Last Updated" dates matter — e.g., 2022 extracts updated through April 2024); preservationists should capture dated versions and the accompanying "Changes for [year]" notes.
- **Continuity risk factors:** the survey depends on (a) triennial PRA re-clearance (next renewal due before August 31, 2027), (b) continued IRS/SOI cooperation for the list sample — arguably its single most irreplaceable input, and (c) appropriations for the ~$7.6M/yr cost. As a voluntary survey not codified in statute, it is more exposed to budget or policy shifts than legislatively mandated censuses.
- **Restricted data:** full-detail microdata are held under CIPSEA and IRS §6103 rules; they are not depositable in public archives, so the public-use files are the only preservable copy for most purposes.

---

## 9. Corrections/Refinements to Your Description

1. ✅ "Triennial cross-sectional" — correct ("normally" is the right hedge: the 1983–86 and 2007–09 panels and 1986/1989 reinterviews are exceptions).
2. ⚠️ "Information is also included from related surveys of pension providers" — this describes the **1989** wave's pension-provider verification survey; it is not part of the modern (1992+) waves. The phrasing matches the ICPSR series description, which spans the older waves.
3. ⚠️ Worth adding: the survey **excludes the Forbes 400**, and the sponsoring partnership with **IRS Statistics of Income** is central to the design (your description omits both).
4. ✅ "No other study for the country collects comparable information" — matches the Fed's own OMB filings: the SCF is "the only source of representative information on the structure of U.S. families' finances."

---

### Key Sources
- Federal Reserve SCF site: federalreserve.gov/econres/scfindex.htm and /scf/scf.htm
- 2022 SCF Codebook: federalreserve.gov/econres/files/codebk2022.txt
- OMB ICR 202408-7100-005 (FR 3059 / 7100-0287): reginfo.gov and omb.report
- Federal Register: 89 FR 16571 (Mar. 7, 2024) and 89 FR 61423 (Jul. 31, 2024)
- NORC project page: norc.org/research/projects/survey-of-consumer-finances.html
- Fed press releases: Feb. 25, 2022 (2022 wave launch); Feb. 28, 2025 (2025 wave launch)
- CRS IF12928, "Analysis of the 2022 Survey of Consumer Finances"
- Kennickell, "The Role of Over-Sampling of the Wealthy in the SCF" (SCF working paper)
- Kuhn, Schularick & Steins (2020), "Income and Wealth Inequality in America, 1949–2016," *JPE* / SCF+
- ICPSR, Survey of Consumer Finances Series (DSDR collection)

## 3. Data Quality

**Evidence for each level:**
- **No Known Issue:** The 2025 wave was designed for **up to 7,000 interviews** (vs. ~4,600 completed in 2022) — an intended *increase* in sample size. ## 4. Statutory Context

**Evidence for each level:**
- **No Known Issue:** Not fully met. The SCF is **not statutorily required** and no statute names it or specifies its contents.
- **Moderate:** Fits squarely: the survey is conducted under the Fed's *general* statutory mission (Federal Reserve Act §2A, 12 U.S.C. §225a; §12A, 12 U.S.C. §263) rather than an explicit mandate, but it is integral to implementing the monetary-policy and financial-stability functions of a federal agency, and — per the Fed's own OMB filings — it is "the only source of representative information on the structure of U.S. families' finances." **No alternative collection substitutes** for it (tax data lack balance sheets; credit-bureau data lack assets; the CPS/ASEC and PSID lack the wealth oversample and asset detail). Programmatic use is deep: FOMC/Fed analysis, Distributional Financial Accounts, Treasury/JCT/CBO modeling.
- **High:** Arguable on "vague authorization" grounds alone, but the absence of substitutes and the clear programmatic use pull it out of High.

**Assessment: Moderate Risk.** The lack of explicit statutory protection means continuation is a discretionary Board decision each cycle — this is the dataset's core structural vulnerability, partially offset by its irreplaceability and its tight coupling to the Fed's statutory mission.

## 5. Staffing and Funding

**Evidence for each level:**
- **No Known Issue:** On funding, clearly met: the Fed is **self-funded and outside the appropriations process** (CRS IF13146), insulating it from congressional/OMB budget cuts that hit BLS, Census, and USDA. The Board's 2025 budget *grew* 11.3%; R&S grew; SCF line grew to $19.8M. The SCF is not dependent on DOGE-driven contract cancellations in the same way appropriated agencies are, though its NORC fieldwork is contract-based.
- **Moderate:** Met on staffing and leadership criteria: (a) In May 2025, Chair Powell announced a **~10% system-wide staff reduction** over "the next couple of years" via attrition, a voluntary deferred-resignation program for Board staff, and a reported hiring freeze (Reuters, Bloomberg, NYT, May 16, 2025) — 10% sits at the boundary of the rubric's 10–39% band, though it is voluntary/attrition-based and not targeted at R&S. (b) **Threatened change in leadership** is clearly present: President Trump repeatedly threatened to fire Chair Powell and attempted to remove Governor Lisa Cook in August 2025 (litigated; Supreme Court allowed her to remain pending argument), and the Powell-era leadership transition at the chair level was scheduled for May 2026.
- **High:** Not met — no 40%+ division losses, no budget cut, and Fed leadership has not been removed (the Cook removal attempt was blocked).

**Assessment: Moderate Risk.** Funding is the strongest in the federal statistical system (self-funded, growing budget), but the rubric's "10–39% staff lost" and "threatened change in leadership" criteria are both triggered at the system/institutional level. There is no evidence the SCF team itself has lost staff, so this is a Moderate rather than High — driven by institutional environment, not dataset-specific harm.

**Overall judgment:** The SCF is currently one of the more resilient federal datasets: fully archived, on schedule, actively funded (self-funded agency; $19.8M in the 2025 field year), with an ICR valid through August 2027 and redundant preservation at ICPSR. Its two genuine vulnerabilities are structural rather than active: (1) it is a *discretionary* survey with no statute requiring its existence, dependent on continued Board discretion and on IRS/SOI cooperation for the wealth oversample; and (2) it sits inside an institution undergoing a 10% workforce drawdown and sustained political pressure on its leadership. Preservationists should treat now as a good time to mirror the complete 1983–2022 series (including codebooks, replicate weights, and the simulated CAPI questionnaire text) and monitor the expected late-2026 2025-wave release as the first concrete test of continuity.
